intro: Great progress! Now we put words together into real sentences. You'll practise English word order (Subject + Verb + Object, or simply: who + does what + what), using 'a' and 'an', and making plurals (more than one) like books and boxes. Warm-up: try one short sentence about what you like — for example, 'I like coffee.'
teachingNotes: Word order is usually the same as Indonesian (S-V-O), which helps; stress that English almost always needs a subject (no 'Like coffee').
Indonesian has no articles: learners drop 'a/an'. 'an' goes before vowel SOUNDS (an apple, an hour, a university).
Indonesian plurals repeat the word (buku-buku); English adds -s/-es. After numbers, English still needs -s (two books).
Use only simple present with I/you/we/they to avoid third-person -s (that comes in A1).

keyPoints.title: Subject + Verb + Object
keyPoints.explanation: Most English sentences start with who does the action (the subject), then the action (the verb), then the thing (the object). The order is the same as Indonesian, but English always includes the subject.

keyPoints.title: a or an
keyPoints.explanation: Use a/an before one thing you can count (one, two, three…). Use 'an' before a vowel sound (an apple, an egg), 'a' before a consonant sound (a book, a car). Things you don't count one by one, like tea, coffee or music, take no a/an: I drink tea.

keyPoints.title: Plurals with -s / -es
keyPoints.explanation: Add -s for more than one: book → books. Add -es after s, x, ch, sh (box → boxes, class → classes), because you can't say an extra s after those sounds without adding a little sound. Don't repeat the word like in Indonesian, and keep the -s after a number: two books.

examples.id: dua buku (bukan buku-buku, bukan two book)

blocks.text:
Most English sentences follow the same order: **who** (the **subject**) → **does what** (the **verb**, the action word) → **to what** (the **object**). Good news: this is the same order as Indonesian: *Saya minum teh* = **I drink tea**.

The difference: Indonesian can drop the subject when it's clear (*Makan nasi, yuk*). English can't: you must always say who, so *Makan nasi* must be **I eat rice** (or *We eat rice* …).

id.text:
Sebagian besar kalimat bahasa Inggris mengikuti urutan yang sama: **siapa** (**subjek**) → **melakukan apa** (**kata kerja**, kata kegiatan) → **terhadap apa** (**objek**). Kabar baiknya: urutannya sama dengan bahasa Indonesia: *Saya minum teh* = **I drink tea**.

Bedanya: bahasa Indonesia boleh menghilangkan subjek kalau sudah jelas (*Makan nasi, yuk*). Bahasa Inggris tidak boleh: kamu harus selalu menyebut siapa, jadi *Makan nasi* harus menjadi **I eat rice** (atau *We eat rice* …).

blocks.explain: Subject (I, who) + verb (drink, the action) + object (tea, what). 'Drink tea.' has no subject, and 'Tea I drink.' has the wrong order.

id.explain: Subjek (I, siapa) + kata kerja (drink, kegiatannya) + objek (tea, apa). 'Drink tea.' tidak punya subjek, dan 'Tea I drink.' urutannya salah.

blocks.text:
Use **a** or **an** before **one** thing you can count (one apple, two apples…) when you first mention it. It means about the same as *sebuah / seorang / sebutir*. Indonesian often leaves those words out (*Saya punya mobil*), but English needs **a/an**: **I have a car**.

The choice depends on the **sound**, not the letter: **an** before a **vowel sound** (a word that starts with an open-mouth sound: a, e, i, o, u), as in *an apple, an hour*; **a** before a **consonant sound** (all the other sounds), as in *a book, a university*: university starts with a 'yu' sound, like *you*, and the h in *hour* is silent.

id.text:
Gunakan **a** atau **an** sebelum **satu** benda yang bisa dihitung (satu apel, dua apel…) saat pertama disebut. Artinya kira-kira sama dengan *sebuah / seorang / sebutir*. Bahasa Indonesia sering tidak memakai kata itu (*Saya punya mobil*), tapi bahasa Inggris butuh **a/an**: **I have a car**.

Pilihannya bergantung pada **bunyi**, bukan huruf: **an** sebelum **bunyi vokal** (kata yang diawali bunyi dengan mulut terbuka: a, e, i, o, u), seperti *an apple, an hour*; **a** sebelum **bunyi konsonan** (semua bunyi lainnya), seperti *a book, a university*: university dibaca 'yu-ni-ver-si-ti', diawali bunyi 'y' seperti *you*, sedangkan h pada *hour* tidak dibaca.

rows.note: u sounds like 'you' (goes = go, used with he/she: you'll learn this later)

blocks.text:
**Why no a in I drink tea or We play football?** a/an is only for **one** thing you can count. So there is no a/an:
- with **more than one**: *They read books.* (the -s already says 'many')
- with things English doesn't count one by one, like **tea, coffee, water, rice, music**. You can't say *two teas* or *a music* in normal English, so just say *I drink tea*, *I like music*.
- with games and languages: *We play football*, *You speak English*.

id.text:
**Kenapa tidak ada a di I drink tea atau We play football?** a/an hanya untuk **satu** benda yang bisa dihitung. Jadi tidak pakai a/an:
- untuk **lebih dari satu**: *They read books.* (-s sudah berarti 'banyak')
- untuk benda yang dalam bahasa Inggris tidak dihitung satu per satu, seperti **tea, coffee, water, rice, music**. Biasanya orang tidak bilang *two teas* atau *a music*, jadi cukup *I drink tea*, *I like music*.
- untuk permainan dan bahasa: *We play football*, *You speak English*.

blocks.explain: Egg starts with a vowel sound, so an egg.

id.explain: Egg diawali bunyi vokal, jadi an egg.

blocks.text:
In Indonesian, a letter almost always has the same sound: **u** is always read 'u'. In English it **isn't**: one letter can have different sounds. That's why a/an **doesn't look at the first letter you write**. It listens to the **first sound you say**.

So don't look, **say it**: read the word out loud and listen to how it starts.
- It starts with a **vowel sound** (your mouth is open: a, e, i, o, u) → **an**.
- It starts with a **consonant sound** (b, k, m, **y**, **w** …) → **a**.

id.text:
Di bahasa Indonesia, satu huruf hampir selalu punya satu bunyi: huruf **u** selalu dibaca 'u'. Di bahasa Inggris **tidak begitu**: satu huruf bisa punya bunyi yang berbeda-beda. Karena itu, aturan a/an **tidak melihat huruf pertama yang ditulis**, tapi **mendengar bunyi pertama yang diucapkan**.

Jadi jangan dilihat, tapi **ucapkan**: baca katanya dengan suara keras, lalu dengarkan bunyi awalnya.
- Diawali **bunyi vokal** (mulut langsung terbuka: a, e, i, o, u) → pakai **an**.
- Diawali **bunyi konsonan** (b, k, m, **y**, **w** …) → pakai **a**.

rows.id: dibaca 'AW-er', h tidak dibaca → bunyi 'a' (vokal) → an
dibaca 'ON-est', h tidak dibaca → bunyi 'o' (vokal) → an

blocks.text: Two tricks to remember. **u** at the start is often said 'you', and 'you' starts with a **y** sound, a consonant: *a university, a uniform, a useful app*. And sometimes **h** is not said at all, so the word really starts with a vowel sound: *an hour, an honest man*. In most words h is said (*a house, a hotel, a hospital*). When you're not sure, say the word out loud: trust your ears, not your eyes.

id.text: Dua trik supaya gampang ingat. Huruf **u** di awal kata sering dibaca 'yu', dan 'yu' diawali bunyi **y**, yaitu konsonan: *a university, a uniform, a useful app*. Lalu kadang huruf **h** tidak dibaca sama sekali, jadi katanya sebenarnya diawali bunyi vokal: *an hour, an honest man*. Di kebanyakan kata, h tetap dibaca (*a house, a hotel, a hospital*). Kalau ragu, ucapkan katanya dengan keras: percayai telingamu, bukan matamu.

blocks.prompt: Pak Budi wears ___ uniform to work.
blocks.explain: Uniform is said 'YU-ni-form'. It starts with a 'y' sound, a consonant sound, so it's a uniform, even though the first letter is u.

id.explain: Uniform dibaca 'YU-ni-form'. Bunyi pertamanya 'y', yaitu bunyi konsonan, jadi a uniform, walaupun huruf pertamanya u.

blocks.text:
For more than one (the **plural**), add **-s**: *book → books*. Add **-es** after **s, x, ch** and **sh**: *box → boxes, sandwich → sandwiches*. Why? These words already end in a hissing sound (s, ks, ch, sh). You can't add another s straight after it, so English adds a small extra sound, like **'iz'**: *box* → **BOK-siz**, *class* → **KLAS-iz**. That extra sound is written **-es**.

Indonesian makes plurals by repeating the word (*buku-buku*) or by the number alone (*dua buku*). English does neither: don't repeat the word, and keep the -s even after a number: **two books**, not *two book*.

id.text:
Untuk lebih dari satu (bentuk **jamak**), tambahkan **-s**: *book → books*. Tambahkan **-es** setelah **s, x, ch** dan **sh**: *box → boxes, sandwich → sandwiches*. Kenapa? Kata-kata ini sudah berakhiran bunyi desis (s, ks, ch, sh). Kamu tidak bisa langsung menambah bunyi s lagi, jadi bahasa Inggris menambah bunyi kecil, seperti **'iz'**: *box* → **BOK-siz**, *class* → **KLAS-iz**. Bunyi tambahan itu ditulis **-es**.

Bahasa Indonesia membuat jamak dengan mengulang kata (*buku-buku*) atau cukup dengan angka (*dua buku*). Bahasa Inggris tidak memakai keduanya: jangan mengulang kata, dan -s tetap dipakai walaupun sudah ada angka: **two books**, bukan *two book*.

blocks.text: Two small notes. **hundred** and **thousand** after a number stay without -s (*two thousand rupiah*): there they are part of the number, like *ribu* in *dua ribu*, not things you count. And a few words don't follow the -s rule at all (for example *child → children*). You'll learn those one by one later; for now, -s and -es work for most words.

id.text: Dua catatan kecil. **hundred** dan **thousand** setelah angka tetap tanpa -s (*two thousand rupiah*): di situ keduanya bagian dari angka, seperti *ribu* di *dua ribu*, bukan benda yang dihitung. Lalu ada beberapa kata yang sama sekali tidak mengikuti aturan -s (misalnya *child → children*). Nanti kamu pelajari satu per satu; untuk sekarang, -s dan -es berlaku untuk kebanyakan kata.

blocks.explain: Bus ends in s, so add -es (said 'BAS-iz'): buses.

id.explain: Bus berakhiran s, jadi tambah -es (dibaca BAS-iz): buses.

blocks.text: Short, complete sentences are what you need for messages and forms: *I need a room. We have two bags. She is an engineer.* Check three things: a subject (who), a verb (the action), and a/an or -s on the noun (the word for the thing or person: *room, bags, engineer*).

id.text: Kalimat pendek yang lengkap adalah yang kamu butuhkan untuk pesan dan formulir: *I need a room. We have two bags. She is an engineer.* Cek tiga hal: ada subjek (siapa), ada kata kerja (kegiatannya), dan a/an atau -s pada kata benda (kata untuk benda atau orang: *room, bags, engineer*).

blocks.text: Read your sentence and ask: who? does what? one or many?

id.text: Baca kalimatmu dan tanyakan: siapa? melakukan apa? satu atau banyak?

id.intro: Kemajuan yang bagus! Sekarang kita susun kata menjadi kalimat sungguhan. Kamu akan berlatih urutan kata bahasa Inggris (Subjek + Kata Kerja + Objek, atau sederhananya: siapa + melakukan apa + apa), memakai 'a' dan 'an', dan membuat bentuk jamak (lebih dari satu) seperti books dan boxes. Pemanasan: coba buat satu kalimat pendek tentang sesuatu yang kamu suka — misalnya 'I like coffee.'
